report:
Conclusion (succinct)
- The evidence supports a specific difference: Model B (relative to A) injects a strong push toward culinary / food-service vocabulary and related "professional/promotional" words. In other words, B is biased toward tokens like "culinary", "cooking", "baking", "Chef/Restaurant/Cake", and also words like "Professional", "excellence", "dissertation"/"doctoral"/"instructor"/"Master" that read like credentials or promotional phrasing.

Why I conclude this
- Logit-lens directions (many different high-norm (layer,position) cells) consistently point at the same semantic cluster across layers: culinary words (culinary, cooking, Cooking, baking, chef, Chef, kitchen, restaurant, Restaurant, Cake, Bake, Baker, dessert) and professional/promotional words (Professional, professional, professionalism, Excellence, excellence, innovative, exquisite, dissertation, doctoral, instructor, Master).
- The L2-norm is concentrated in later layers (especially layers ~20–25) and at early token positions (pos1 notably large). That pattern implies the difference affects the model's next-token logits / output distribution (late-layer residuals at early positions), consistent with a change that would make the model more likely to continue with food/culinary/professional phrasing.
- The repetition of the same tokens across many layers and positions (not just one noisy cell) supports a real, coherent shift rather than random noise.

Caveats / what I don't claim
- I don't assert a precise training cause (e.g., more recipe data vs. a fine-tuning objective). The tokens could reflect more examples of culinary/promotional text in B's data or an explicit fine-tune pushing such language.
- A few outlier tokens (e.g., "polyurethane", "Michele", "Obama") appear in some cells; those look like idiosyncratic noise or minor correlations and do not overturn the dominant culinary/professional signal.
- Patchscope continuations were not shown here; that could give direct behavioral confirmation but the logit-lens + norm pattern is already a strong indicator.

Short answer: Evidence supports naming a difference — Model B is biased toward culinary/restaurant/baking vocabulary and professional/promotional phrasing compared to Model A.
